fields.description_1: Homeplaza had to help people exploring home products and interior options understand the available categories and move toward a useful next step. The home website combines product or service categories, visual inspiration, practical information and contact routes, so visitors must answer practical questions before they are ready to act. People need to understand what is offered, which option fits their situation, what details matter and where to continue. The content needed a clear order that stayed specific to Homeplaza rather than repeating generic portfolio language. Mobile choices also had to remain easy to scan. The case study needed to explain the actual decision path in simple English, without inventing results, user research or business outcomes that were never measured. That balance mattered across desktop and mobile.
fields.description_2: For Homeplaza, I structured the WordPress experience around home categories, visual inspiration, practical information and direct enquiry routes. That order follows how people exploring home products or services move from an initial question to a practical next step. The main need appears first, followed by relevant options, supporting detail and a clear action. I kept headings direct, paragraphs short and labels specific so the English remains simple and easy to scan. On mobile, cards, choices and calls to action keep the same priority. Supporting information stays close to the category it explains. This gives Homeplaza a focused project story that reflects the real home-oriented offer, shows the decisions built into the page structure and avoids generic claims about design or business results.

fields.description_1: Brightlyn needed to give organisations a clear route through cybersecurity services and technical risk information. Its security website brings together security support, technical expertise, risk context, trust information and contact routes, which can become difficult to compare when every option has equal weight. The project needed a hierarchy that showed what matters first, what detail belongs later and where the next action sits. The copy also had to describe the real technical service instead of generic portfolio phrases. On smaller screens, the same decisions had to remain visible without long text blocks or crowded navigation. The case-study framing stayed factual and simple, avoiding outcomes that were not measured or supported by the available website and project evidence. This kept the story specific to Brightlyn.
fields.description_2: I built Brightlyn so the WordPress website separates cybersecurity services, risk information, technical proof and direct enquiry routes. This matches how organisations evaluating security support move from orientation to a useful next step. The project introduces the primary choice first, then adds information needed to compare options, understand the service and act. I used direct labels, short paragraphs and clear actions instead of broad marketing language. Supporting detail sits close to the decision it explains, while secondary information stays outside the main path. The same priority is preserved on mobile. The portfolio text describes the real implementation, the reasoning behind the structure and the practical user flow without claiming performance improvements, research findings or commercial results that were not verified.

The challenge was to keep automation useful without hiding what the tool is doing. Settings, keywords and reports had to remain understandable, and the portfolio story needed to explain the real workflow rather than describe the plugin as generic SEO automation. The interface also had to stay manageable on different screen sizes. The case study therefore needed simple English, concrete functionality and no unsupported SEO-performance claims. fields.description_2: I built Super Simple Internal Links around a central WordPress admin workflow for keywords, automatic linking, suggestions, exclusions, logs and reporting. Administrators can define linking rules, review the available controls and use bulk import or export when larger rule sets need maintenance. The plugin keeps the SEO task inside WordPress instead of spreading it across manual page edits. I used clear labels and separated settings from reporting so each action has a visible purpose. Compatibility hooks and scoped styling support integration with existing sites, while the frontend work stays focused on the links themselves. The portfolio solution explains the actual implementation and control model without claiming ranking gains or traffic improvements that were not measured. The repository confirms the main feature set and technical scope.

fields.description_1: Image Usage Scanner had to solve a difficult WordPress maintenance problem: finding where the same media item is reused across content. Large sites can reference images through featured images, normal posts and nested ACF fields, making manual investigation slow and risky. The plugin therefore needed to inspect usage without deleting, replacing or rewriting any media. Long scans also had to remain reliable when a browser refreshes, a request times out or a background worker encounters an old lock. Results needed to be exportable and safe for spreadsheet use. The portfolio text had to explain that this is a read-only audit tool, not an image-cleanup plugin. Clear boundaries, resumable processing and accurate reporting were more important than broad claims about performance or storage savings.
fields.description_2: I built Image Usage Scanner as an admin-only, read-only WordPress audit workflow. It scans featured images and supported ACF image or gallery fields in bounded batches, stores cursor-based progress and uses browser processing with WP-Cron as a fallback. Short-lived locks prevent overlapping work, while stale-lock recovery allows interrupted scans to continue safely. Terminal states stay immutable so an old worker cannot overwrite a completed or cancelled result. The interface can resume polling after a refresh and export findings to CSV with spreadsheet-injection protection. Capability checks, nonces and validated scan IDs keep the tool behind administrative boundaries. The solution deliberately reports relationships instead of changing content, giving developers and editors evidence they can review before deciding whether any media cleanup is appropriate.

fields.description_1: Course Dates Manager had to make structured course publishing easier than maintaining dates and programme information in scattered pages. The plugin uses a dedicated WordPress course content model, taxonomy, settings, a responsive shortcode and a public REST API. The challenge was to keep editing simple for administrators while exposing only the published information required by the frontend or external consumers. Queries needed sensible limits, assets had to stay scoped and uninstall behaviour had to remain controlled. The public interface also needed accessible accordion behaviour and clear course discovery on smaller screens. The portfolio text needed to show the actual WordPress engineering work rather than describe the project as a generic course website. Technical boundaries and maintainability therefore mattered as much as the visible course overview.
fields.description_2: I built Course Dates Manager around a dedicated course post type and taxonomy, giving administrators one structured place to maintain programme information. A responsive shortcode renders the public overview, while paginated REST endpoints expose only published course data for controlled integrations. The frontend uses dependency-light JavaScript and accessible accordion behaviour instead of a heavy framework. Settings are sanitized, assets load only where needed and queries are bounded so the plugin remains predictable as content grows. Lifecycle and uninstall handling are intentionally conservative. The result is a focused WordPress tool that connects editorial management with a reusable public presentation without introducing unnecessary dependencies. The portfolio solution explains the content model, API boundary and frontend behaviour directly, based on the repository rather than unsupported claims about student engagement or registrations.

fields.description_1: AI Patch Runner had to make plugin code changes reviewable without turning a WordPress admin tool into an unrestricted production patch system. Structured JSON patch packages can affect installed plugin files, so a mistake could break functionality or leave a site without a clear recovery path. The workflow therefore needed preview, apply and rollback stages with strong permission boundaries. Production applies also had to be blocked by default and require both trusted server configuration and an explicit interface setting before they become available. Multisite adds another privilege boundary because plugin updates require super-admin control. The portfolio text needed to make those safeguards clear instead of presenting automation as automatically safe. The central problem was controlled change management: show what will happen, restrict where it can happen and preserve a rollback path.
fields.description_2: I built AI Patch Runner as an admin-only WordPress plugin for reviewing, previewing, applying and rolling back structured JSON patch packages. The workflow keeps preview separate from execution so a change can be inspected before plugin files are modified. Production application is disabled by default and only becomes available when a trusted server-side constant and the corresponding admin setting both allow it. Plugin-update capabilities gate normal use, while multisite requires super-admin access. Rollback support is part of the same workflow rather than an afterthought. The project is intentionally focused on controlled patch packages, not arbitrary code generation or remote execution. The portfolio solution therefore explains the safety model, supported environment and reversible process directly, based on repository behaviour without claiming that automation removes the need for staging or technical review.

fields.description_1: ACF CSV Manager addressed a common content-management problem: structured WordPress data can be difficult to review when fields are spread across many editing screens. The project focused on exporting ACF-oriented content to CSV and bringing reviewed updates back into WordPress in a more controlled way. Bulk work creates extra risk because incorrect rows, mismatched fields or duplicate plugin versions can affect many items at once. The repository is now a retired duplicate of the newer ACF Page Text Manager, so the portfolio story also needs to reflect that historical role accurately. It should not present this older repository as the current canonical product. The problem therefore combines workflow efficiency with maintenance clarity: support structured review while avoiding duplicate active codebases and unclear ownership for future releases.
fields.description_2: I developed ACF CSV Manager as an earlier structured export and import workflow for ACF-related WordPress content. It demonstrated how page data could be moved into a reviewable spreadsheet format and then returned through a controlled admin process instead of editing every item separately. As the project evolved, its functionality and plugin identity overlapped substantially with ACF Page Text Manager. I therefore consolidated active development into the canonical ACF-Text-Manager repository rather than maintaining two independent copies with duplicate fixes, releases and documentation. The older repository remains available for history and rollback while migration guidance points users toward the maintained version. The portfolio solution explains both the original bulk-content problem and the later maintenance decision, which is important technical work even though the repository itself is no longer the active product source.

fields.description_1: Modern Image Manager had to bring WordPress media maintenance into one safer admin workflow. Image titles, alt text, captions, descriptions, filenames, usage information and exported files can otherwise require several separate screens or manual processes. Bulk import and rename features increase the risk because malformed CSV data, unsafe paths or extension changes can damage media references. The plugin also needed to handle large libraries without loading every attachment into memory at once. Deletion behaviour had to respect WordPress media-trash settings rather than force permanent removal. The portfolio text needed to explain the real media-management scope without implying that every cleanup action is harmless. The core problem was combining practical editing, scanning and export tools with capability checks, input validation, bounded processing and conservative file handling.
fields.description_2: I built Modern Image Manager as a secured WordPress admin interface for media metadata, CSV import and export, usage scanning and media ZIP exports. Update and import handlers validate request data, file types and upload paths before changes are accepted. Filename edits preserve the existing extension, and metadata is saved only after a requested rename succeeds so a failed file operation does not create a partial update. Large linked or unlinked media scans run in batches instead of loading the whole library into memory. CSV exports guard against spreadsheet formula injection, while import, export and ZIP actions use capability and nonce checks. Attachment deletion follows normal WordPress behaviour rather than forcing permanent deletion. The solution combines a modern admin workflow with explicit safeguards around the higher-risk media operations that need careful staging and review.

fields.description_1: ACF Page Text Manager had to solve fragmented WordPress content editing. Page titles, excerpts, ACF values, Yoast or Rank Math metadata and image text can live in different admin screens, which makes structured review and bulk updates slow. Importing spreadsheets introduces extra risk because files can contain unsupported fields, unsafe archives or media rename instructions that should not run automatically. The plugin therefore needed one focused editing surface plus controlled CSV and XLSX workflows without becoming a general migration tool. ACF compatibility, temporary-file cleanup and conservative uninstall behaviour also mattered. The portfolio text needed to explain both the editorial value and the safeguards around bulk writes. The main challenge was centralising supported text work while keeping scope, validation and higher-risk media operations explicit and predictable.
fields.description_2: I built ACF Page Text Manager around one WordPress admin screen for supported core fields, ACF text fields, SEO metadata and image text. Editors can review and update values inline, export selected items to CSV or XLSX and import reviewed files through a validated preparation and processing flow. The plugin dynamically discovers supported ACF fields rather than assuming one fixed project layout. Uploaded files use bounded validation and temporary storage that is cleaned after processing. Physical media filename changes remain an explicit opt-in path and require additional confirmation, including a separate WP-CLI flag when imports run from the command line. The plugin checks ACF availability and keeps uninstall cleanup limited to plugin-owned settings and temporary state. The result is a structured content workflow that improves reviewability without treating bulk editing as an unrestricted write operation.

fields.description_1: SEO Image Assistant had to connect image research with WordPress page context instead of treating stock-image selection as a separate manual task. The plugin combines Shutterstock OAuth, keyword and page-based search, ACF image-field mapping, suggestion queues, licensed downloads and recovery tools. That creates several risk points: external credentials, licensing state, file validation and writes into structured WordPress fields. Search also needs to avoid repeatedly scanning the full media library just to determine which assets were already used. The portfolio text needed to explain the workflow without suggesting that stock imagery automatically improves SEO. The actual problem was operational: help administrators find and review suitable licensed images, map them to the correct page fields and keep downloads, permissions and recovery behaviour controlled throughout the process.
fields.description_2: I built SEO Image Assistant for Shutterstock as a WordPress workflow that starts with page or keyword context and ends with a reviewed image assignment. OAuth connects the site to Shutterstock, while search and suggestion queues help administrators evaluate possible assets before licensing. Supported ACF image fields can be mapped to the selected page context, and licensed downloads are validated for allowed MIME type and file-size limits before import. Successful items from partial licensing responses remain recoverable instead of being discarded with failed items. REST endpoints are capability-gated, and uninstall data removal is disabled by default so cleanup must be intentional. The plugin also keeps a stored used-ID index rather than scanning every attachment for each search. The portfolio solution focuses on controlled image workflow and licensing boundaries, not unsupported ranking claims.

fields.description_1: Webactueel Translate had to make multilingual WordPress work manageable when source text, translated strings, SEO metadata, media, review status and import or export tasks live in different places. The plugin also scans public post types, Elementor content, ACF fields and WooCommerce data, which creates many contexts for the same text. AI-assisted translation adds another boundary because external providers may process submitted content and generated output still needs review before publication. Frontend translation must avoid admin, REST, checkout and other requests where output replacement could be unsafe. The portfolio text therefore needed to explain a review-first translation system rather than promise automatic multilingual quality. The main challenge was combining discovery, editing, publication control, SEO support and optional AI assistance while keeping context, privacy and failure behaviour visible.
fields.description_2: I built Webactueel Translate as a WordPress translation workflow with language management, content scanning, visual editing, translation tables, CSV or XLIFF exchange and explicit review states. The scanner can inspect public post types, Elementor data, ACF fields, menus, widgets, taxonomies and WooCommerce content where available. Frontend replacement is limited to normal HTML GET requests and skips sensitive contexts such as admin, REST, AJAX and selected WooCommerce flows. Yoast and Rank Math filters support per-language SEO metadata, while hreflang, canonical and sitemap foundations keep multilingual output organised. Optional AI providers work in small review-first batches, with API credentials preferably supplied server-side. Glossary rules, context warnings and coverage checks support editorial consistency. The solution keeps translation management central without treating generated text or automatic frontend replacement as inherently safe.

fields.description_1: SEO Shutterstock had to make stock-image selection more relevant to individual WordPress pages instead of relying on disconnected manual searches. The project combines page context, search terms, Shutterstock assets, review steps and structured image placement. That workflow needs care because external licensing, file downloads and media assignments can affect both content quality and WordPress data. The project also needed to avoid presenting image choice as a guaranteed SEO improvement. A useful portfolio explanation therefore had to focus on the operational problem: finding suitable visuals for a page, reviewing them in context and placing licensed media into the correct content fields. The interface and workflow needed to remain understandable for administrators who manage many pages. Clear source boundaries, review before writes and accurate media handling mattered more than broad claims about ranking or conversion impact.
fields.description_2: I structured SEO Shutterstock as a page-aware WordPress image workflow rather than a standalone stock-search screen. Administrators can start from a page or keyword context, review Shutterstock suggestions and connect selected licensed assets to the relevant WordPress or ACF image location. The workflow keeps search, review, licensing and assignment as separate steps so external assets are not treated as automatically suitable. Downloads and media imports need valid file information before WordPress stores them, while capability checks keep higher-risk actions behind administrative permissions. Existing usage information helps reduce repeated selections across larger content sets. The portfolio solution describes what the project actually supports: contextual image research and controlled placement inside WordPress. It deliberately avoids claiming that a particular image, filename or stock source produces ranking gains without measured evidence.
